stories.fact: Invented by accident in 1968 at 3M when Spencer Silver tried to make a super-strong adhesive, but created a weak, reusable one instead.
Slack started as an internal chat tool built by Stewart Butterfield's team while they were developing a failed video game called 'Glitch'.
The first computer mouse was invented in 1964 by Douglas Engelbart and was carved out of a block of wood with two metallic wheels.
Designed by Christopher Sholes in 1873 to slow typists down slightly and prevent mechanical typewriter arms from jamming together.
The term 'Wi-Fi' does not stand for 'Wireless Fidelity'; it was created purely as a catchy marketing name by Interbrand in 1999.
Before 1995, registering domain names on the internet was completely free.
Named after King Harald 'Bluetooth' Gormsson, a 10th-century Scandinavian king who united Scandinavia, just as Bluetooth unites tech devices.
Sent in 1971 by Ray Tomlinson to himself, introducing the '@' symbol to separate the user name from the host computer name.
Invented in 1957 by Alfred Fielding and Marc Chavannes as textured 3D plastic wallpaper before finding its purpose in packaging.
Popularized in 1926 by Henry Ford, who reduced hours from 48 to 40 after discovering well-rested workers produced more without safety errors.
Founded in 1889 by Fusajiro Yamauchi as a handmade playing card (Hanafuda) company in Kyoto, Japan.
The world's first webcam was created at Cambridge University in 1991 simply to monitor whether the Trojan Room coffee pot was full or empty.
Originally launched on Valentine's Day in 2005 as a video-based online dating site before pivoting to general video sharing.
Twitter was born out of a day-long brainstorming session at Odeo, a podcasting company trying to reinvent itself when iTunes launched.
Created in 2006 by Daniel Ek and Martin Lorentzon in Sweden as a legal alternative to music piracy like Napster and Pirate Bay.
Discovered accidentally in 1945 when Percy Spencer noticed a radar magnetron melted a chocolate candy bar in his pocket.
Originally named Confinity in 1998, it was designed to transfer money via Palm Pilots before focusing on Web transactions.
Created during WWII when James Wright tried to invent a synthetic rubber substitute for the US government using silicone oil.
Started as 'Burbn', a complex check-in app with gaming features, before the creators stripped away everything except photo-sharing with filters.
Jeff Bezos originally considered naming the company 'Cadabra' (as in Incantations), but his lawyer misheard it as 'Cadaver'.
Originally named 'Oak' after an oak tree that stood outside creator James Gosling's office at Sun Microsystems.
Named after 'googol' (1 followed by 100 zeros), but misspelling it on a domain registration check stuck as the permanent name.
Originated in Germany in the 1950s as 'Bürolandschaft' (office landscape), intended to break down social hierarchies and foster organic interaction.
Designed by Robert Propst in 1964 as the 'Action Office' to give workers privacy, but later mass-produced into rigid corporate pods.
Myth says it was named after Room 404 at CERN where the World Wide Web originated, but 404 was simply a standard HTTP response code.
Derived from the famous 1970 Monty Python sketch where characters endlessly repeat 'Spam', symbolizing annoying, repetitive noise.
Developed at Carnegie Mellon in 2000 to prevent bot spam, later repurposed (reCAPTCHA) to digitize scanned books using human efforts.
Popularized in 1947 when Grace Hopper found a real moth stuck in a relay of the Harvard Mark II computer, taping it into the logbook.
Developed as a standalone iOS app at SRI International before Apple acquired it in 2010; 'Siri' means 'beautiful woman who leads you to victory' in Norwegian.
Features Sir Isaac Newton sitting under an apple tree, drawn by Apple co-founder Ronald Wayne in 1976.
Originally named 'Tokyo Tsushin Kogyo', the company changed its name to Sony in 1958, blending Latin 'sonus' (sound) and slang 'sonny' (boy).
Founded in 1865 as a single wood pulp mill on the banks of the Nokianvirta river in Finland, long before telecommunications.
Originally founded in 2003 to build a smart operating system for digital cameras before pivoting to compete with Symbian and Windows Mobile.
Suggested for Twitter in 2007 by Chris Messina to group related messages, though Twitter initially rejected the idea as 'too nerdy'.
Originated in Hawaii in 1966 when the Hawaiian Fashion Guild promoted 'Aloha Fridays' to encourage wearing local shirts to work.
Popularized in the 1930s after the invention of the electric water cooler, which became the natural gathering spot for office workers.
Created in 1987 by brothers Thomas and John Knoll as a display program called 'Display' to view grayscale images on a Mac.
Co-founder Reed Hastings got the idea after paying a $40 late fee for a rented copy of 'Apollo 13' from Blockbuster.
Started when founders Brian Chesky and Joe Gebbia put air mattresses in their living room to help pay rent during a San Francisco design conference.
Launched out of Reid Hoffman's living room in late 2002 with a mission to connect the world's professionals.
Originally named 'AuctionWeb' in 1995; the first item ever sold was a broken laser pointer for $14.83 to a collector of broken lasers.
Conceived in 1965 by copywriter Rudy Perz, who imagined a little flour character popping out of a crescent roll can.
Founded in Switzerland in 1981; the name comes from 'logiciel', the French word for software.
Created by Facebook co-founder Dustin Moskovitz and engineer Justin Rosenstein to streamline Facebook's internal workflow and eliminate meetings.
Founded in 2011 by Eric Yuan, who grew frustrated while working at Cisco WebEx because the video system was clunky and customer satisfaction was low.
Created by Fog Creek Software in 2011, inspired by physical Kanban whiteboards used in manufacturing plants.
Institutionalized during WWII in factories, and legally recognized in 1952 when the Pan-American Coffee Bureau launched a massive advertising campaign.
Gained massive adoption during WWII at defense plants like DuPont and Boeing to protect military manufacturing secrets.
Created by Guido van Rossum in 1989, who named the language after the British comedy troupe 'Monty Python's Flying Circus'.
Created in 1991 by Finnish university student Linus Torvalds as a free, personal hobby project that grew into the world's largest open-source OS.
Bill Hewlett and Dave Packard flipped a coin in 1939 to decide whether their company would be named Hewlett-Packard or Packard-Hewlett.
Invented in the late 1950s by Martin Heit, a photographer who realized he could write on film negatives with a marker and wipe them clean.
Invented in 1956 by typist Bette Nesmith Graham in her kitchen using tempera water paint to hide typing errors.
Before rubber erasers were patented in 1770, people used rolled-up pieces of white bread to erase pencil marks.
Invented by Hungarian journalist László Bíró in 1931 because fountain pen ink smudged easily and took too long to dry on newsprint.
The ubiquitous 'Gem' paperclip was never patented, but gained dominance in the late 1890s because it held paper without tearing it.
Introduced on the Remington No. 2 typewriter in 1878, allowing a single key to alternate between lowercase and uppercase letters.
The phrase 'word processing' was coined by IBM in the late 1960s to market their magnetic tape typewriters.
Synthesized in 1965 by Stephanie Kwolek at DuPont while searching for a lightweight fiber for strong, fuel-efficient tires.
Invented in 1941 by George de Mestral after noticing burrs sticking to his clothing and dog's fur after a hunting trip.
Accidentally discovered in 1938 by Roy J. Plunkett while researching refrigerants at DuPont's Jackson Laboratory.
Patented in 1986 by Chuck Hull, who founded 3D Systems and invented Stereolithography (SLA).
Invented in 1994 by Masahiro Hara at Denso Wave, a Japanese automotive company, to quickly track auto components during assembly.
Conceived in 1948 by Norman Joseph Woodland, who drew lines in the sand at the beach to represent Morse code visually.
Developed by the US Department of Defense in 1973 for military navigation, then made fully available for global civilian use in the 1990s.
Created in 1996 by a consortium of tech companies led by Intel's Ajay Bhatt to replace cumbersome serial and parallel ports.
Developed by Robert Metcalfe at Xerox PARC in 1973, inspired by ALOHANET, an early wireless radio network in Hawaii.
Invented by Fujio Masuoka at Toshiba in 1980; the name 'flash' was suggested because the erasure process resembled a camera flash.
Created by IBM in 1967 as an 8-inch disk, designed to load microcode into mainframe systems cheaply.
Invented by Gary Starkweather at Xerox PARC in 1969 by modifying an existing xerographic copier with a laser beam.
IBM created the first hard drive in 1956 (RAMAC 305); it was the size of two refrigerators and stored 5 Megabytes of data.
The first SMS was sent on December 3, 1992, by engineer Neil Papworth, reading 'Merry Christmas' from a PC to an Orbitel 901 phone.
Created in 1987 by Steve Wilhite at CompuServe as a color image format that wouldn't consume massive bandwidth over dial-up.
Designed in 1995 as an open-source replacement for GIF after Unisys announced it would enforce patents on the LZW compression algorithm.
Created in just 10 days in May 1995 by Brendan Eich while working at Netscape Communications.
Proposed by Håkon Wium Lie in 1994 while working with Tim Berners-Lee at CERN to separate content from design on web pages.
Invented in 1989 by Sir Tim Berners-Lee at CERN to facilitate automated information sharing between scientists worldwide.
The codename 'Mozilla' was created at Netscape in 1994 as a combination of 'Mosaic killer' and 'Godzilla'.
Named after co-founder Marc Ewing's red Cornell University lacrosse cap, which he wore while assisting students with computer problems.
Created in 2012 by Eben Upton's team at Cambridge to inspire basic computer science education for young students with an affordable $25 board.
Created in 2005 in Ivrea, Italy, to provide design students with a low-cost microcontroller platform; named after a local pub where the founders met.
Pioneered in the late 1990s by Salesforce, which launched a famous 'End of Software' marketing campaign with anti-software protest rallies.
Created in 2001 when 17 software developers gathered at a ski resort in Utah to write the 'Agile Manifesto' for lighter project management.
Developed by Jeff Sutherland and Ken Schwaber in 1993; the term 'Scrum' was borrowed from a 1986 Harvard Business Review article about rugby.
Popularized by Extreme Programming (XP) in the 1990s, forcing attendees to remain standing to keep status updates short and focused.
Originated in the 1940s as occupational alcohol programs to reduce absenteeism in manufacturing plants.
Systematized during WWI by the US Military as merit rating systems to identify candidates for promotion.
Attributed to Leonardo da Vinci in 1482, who wrote a letter to the Duke of Milan highlighting his military engineering skills.
Emerged after WWII as US companies expanded rapidly and required external specialists to recruit high-level management talent.
Invented in 1967 by Christel Kammerer in Germany to help working mothers balance employment with family commitments.
Coined by Jack Nilles in 1973 during the OPEC oil crisis as a solution to reduce long commuting times and conserve fuel.
The first modern co-working space, 'Spiralförmig', was opened in Berlin in 1995 by hackers who shared physical workspace and internet costs.
Designed by Bill Stumpf and Don Chadwick for Herman Miller in 1994, resulting in the iconic Aeron chair based on human physiology.
Used historically by figures like Thomas Jefferson and Ernest Hemingway, but modern adoption surged in the 2010s due to sedentary health studies.
Founded in 2007 by Robert Hohman, Rich Barton, and Tim Besse after Hohman accidentally printed employee feedback and salary data on a shared office printer.
Started by Melanie Perkins in Australia in 2013 after she spent years teaching university students complex graphic design tools and realizing a simpler solution was needed.
Founded by Ivan Zhao and Simon Last in 2013, but rebuilt completely from scratch in Kyoto, Japan, in 2015 after initial app crashes.
Created in 2011 by Luis von Ahn and Severin Hacker to provide free language education while crowdsourcing translation for news articles.
Conceived by Drew Houston in 2007 while sitting on a bus ride from Boston to New York, realized he had forgotten his USB thumb drive at home.
Started in 2012 by Dylan Field and Evan Wallace while studying at Brown University, aiming to build browser-based design tools using WebGL.
